item.title: U.S. approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
[Reuters] The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive. The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada. On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots – the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles. Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,000 households in the Kyiv region following Russian strikes on Friday night. He accused Russia of "deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure every day". The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel. The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east. Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October. In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe". It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale". Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph. The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine. [BBC] Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies that the country was running critically low on. In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now". He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks. Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran. It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine. Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence. In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles - three weeks after offering the country such a right. Additional reporting by Victoria Bourne After deadly Kyiv strike, Ukraine warns interceptor shortage is costing lives Trump now 'not sure' about letting Ukraine build Patriot missiles This article originally appeared on BBC at https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c3vgxznlx7jzo?xtor=AL-72-%5Bpartner%5D-%5Byahoo.north.america%5D-%5Bheadline%5D-%5Bnews%5D-%5Bbizdev%5D-%5Bisapi%5D

item.title: D.C. and Virginia sue to stop Trump's massive arch days before construction
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The D.C. government and the commonwealth of Virginia sued Saturday to block construction of President Donald Trump’s planned triumphal arch, calling it a “flagrantly unlawful” project that will forever change the landscape of the nation’s capital. The lawsuit is the latest attempt to stop the 250-foot-tall arch, which Trump hopes to build near Arlington National Cemetery and says will commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday. The administration would like to begin construction as soon as next week. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The two jurisdictions are asking U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan to halt the plan and argue that they have “indisputable standing” to bring their lawsuit because the towering arch would have tangible, negative effects on the region - an argument that distinguishes their lawsuit from others that have tried to stop Trump’s construction projects. D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb (D) said the arch construction would cause “serious, immediate and irreparable harm to the District and its residents,” while Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones (D) said “Trump’s illegal vanity project” would be an affront to Arlington National Cemetery and the “extraordinary sacrifices it represents.” “The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place,” Jones said in a statement. “We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice.” The arch already faces legal peril. In a separate case brought by three Vietnam War veterans and a historic preservationist, Chutkan on Friday signaled she might block it. Asked about the lawsuit, a White House spokesman reiterated the administration’s position that the arch would be “one of the most iconic landmarks” in the world. Spokespeople for the Interior Department, which is managing the project, did not immediately respond to questions about the new lawsuit. The administration has acknowledged that the arch will unavoidably harm local historic sites by altering views, and that it will divert traffic and create loud noise during years of planned construction, among other disruptions. Officials have said that those harms are not significant enough to halt what the administration has deemed a “high-priority project.” The Trump administration has also tried to defend the arch and the president’s other construction projects by claiming that litigants lack standing - the legal grounds to sue - because they cannot show that they would be directly harmed. That argument swayed the Supreme Court this summer in a case about Trump’s White House ballroom. The justices ruled 5-4 that a historic preservationist likely could not prove that she would be harmed by the project - and cleared the way for Trump to keep building. D.C. and Virginia say harms to the region would be irreversible if Trump’s project proceeds. In their court filing, the jurisdictions argue that the arch would harm the region’s security and emergency preparedness, disrupt traffic, degrade the environment and run afoul of the Height Act, which caps building heights at 130 feet in D.C. - a defining feature of the city’s architecture intended to preserve views of the Washington Monument and the U.S. Capitol. The arch would be nearly double that height. They also say the arch is illegal because Congress has not authorized it, and because the National Park Service failed to follow laws requiring “appropriate consultation before undertaking a project that would transform the District’s physical landscape and upend its historic plan.” The Trump administration has said construction could begin by Thursday if the National Capital Planning Commission - a federal review panel that oversees major projects in the region - approves the arch proposal at its meeting that day. Trump has packed the commission with allies, and its chairman has already said he plans to vote for the project. The Interior Department could then quickly green-light construction, officials have said. Lawyers for D.C. and Virginia argue that if the court fails to act now, the administration could swiftly shift to a new argument - as officials did last year with Trump’s ballroom - that once construction on project begins, it will be too late to stop. “The court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed,” they wrote in the filing. D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson (D), who has served on the National Capital Planning Commission since 2012, wrote in a declaration to the court that the speed of the commission’s review has been “unprecedented” and insufficient. The commission advanced the proposed arch through key reviews within five weeks, compared with the years-long process to evaluate typical projects, he said. “Congress established a process for approving memorials in Washington for good reason. What we commemorate, where we commemorate it, and how a memorial fits into Washington’s historic landscape are important decisions that deserve careful consideration,” Mendelson said in an accompanying statement. “The proposed Arch has not gone through that process.” Trump has said he hopes to build the arch on Memorial Circle, a traffic roundabout near the south end of Arlington Memorial Bridge and tucked inside Washington’s boundaries. Administration officials have laid out a plan to work 20 hours per day, year-round, for several years to construct the arch. The speed and scope of the president’s project - a planned five-level “concrete structure clad in granite,” as federal officials have described it - have alarmed historic preservationists, architects, parks advocates and local groups that say its effects on the region would be irrevocable. The arch would permanently disrupt historic architectural designs by competing with the Washington Monument, local officials argue. It would also obstruct the sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, a memorial to Robert E. Lee. The historic preservation officers from both jurisdictions have raised concerns about a lack of review required by law. But the arch would also cause other logistical headaches, D.C. and Virginia officials say, such as year-round construction for two to three years that would temporarily and permanently change traffic patterns on a busy artery - with potentially serious implications. They note the arch construction could hamper emergency vehicles at the foot of a bridge that is a designated evacuation route. “The construction-related closures of the Circle, new pedestrian crossings, and additional pedestrian and vehicular traffic after construction is finished will all complicate evacuations from and emergency response in the District,” they write. And in a highly restricted airspace, the towering height of the proposed arch would “pose risks to air safety,” which will require local officials to spend significant resources adjusting emergency preparedness plans, D.C. and Virginia officials say. D.C. leaders have not previously sued to block Trump’s construction projects, including the ballroom, the changes to the East Potomac golf course and other projects that have drawn complaints. In a hearing Friday in the separate lawsuit seeking to block the arch, Chutkan independently raised questions about how the arch would affect traffic patterns and other potential disruptions to the region. An administration lawyer told the judge that he was not prepared to talk about traffic patterns because that issue was not germane to that case. Chutkan questioned what harm would be caused by waiting several months versus beginning construction as soon as next week. “What is the rush to put this arch up?” she asked. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2026/10/31/dc-virginia-sue-block-trumps-proposed-triumphal-arch/

item.title: Google could join Trump's $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense project
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Bloomberg) -- Alphabet Inc.’s Google is in talks with the US Defense Department to work on a new data security effort underpinning the $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense program, according to people familiar with the matter. Most Read from Bloomberg Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist Stocks Slump as Wall Street Gets AI Wake-Up Call: Markets Wrap Google Erases a Record $500 Billion as AI Eats Into Sales Kushner’s Thrive Holdings to Buy ADT for $7.6 Billion in Cash Intel Suffers Worst Stock Drop in Decades on Weak Forecast The Pentagon is standing up a new industry group that aims to secure the data that feeds into military software being built for Golden Dome, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the matter isn’t public. The group is likely to involve multiple companies working to ensure data that flows into the new command-and-control software is resilient to attacks, such as attempts to cut access to landlines, cell towers and other critical communications infrastructure, the people said. The talks have focused on Google’s data storage, networking and cybersecurity capabilities, one of the people said. Conversations are still early and plans could change, they said. Aalyria Technologies Inc., a networking company spun out from Google, is involved in the consortium, they added. A Pentagon official said that while the office may explore preliminary concepts, no final decision has been made regarding a new consortium or industry participants. Google and Aalyria declined to comment. Golden Dome is President Donald Trump’s marquee defense program to build a layer of defense systems from ground to space that will protect the US from foreign attack. The Golden Dome’s command-and-control layer, which is being developed by a separate group including Anduril, Palantir and SpaceX, is intended to control and connect weapons systems, radars, and other previously siloed systems across the US military. The effort would mark Google’s first publicly known involvement in the Golden Dome program and another sign of how the search engine giant is continuing to lean into national security and defense work. Both the Pentagon’s separate Golden Dome initiatives to pioneer space-based missile interceptors and its command-and-control consortium rely on numerous companies from startups to established primes, unlike past defense programs that have been more typically anchored by a single, large contractor. Google has had a complicated history with defense work. In 2018, thousands of Google employees protested the company’s involvement in a military AI program called Project Maven, citing concerns that the commercial technology would be supporting warfare. Google ultimately didn’t renew the contract. In the years since, however, the company has created a dedicated public sector business and signed deals with the military for AI and cloud capabilities. In April, Google signed an agreement to use its AI models for classified work at the Pentagon, an about-face from its previous stance amid another, albeit smaller, backlash from employees. item.title: FBI questions donors as 2 Dan Sullivans compete in Alaska Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The FBI has begun reaching out to donors of Dan J. Sullivan asking about potential deception, as federal authorities ramped up their investigation of the U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska who shares a name with the Republican incumbent. Agents have contacted donors in at least two remote communities in Alaska and a couple in Massachusetts . An Anchorage-based FBI agent visited a boat dealership in Petersburg, a small fishing community accessible only by air or water where the candidate lives. The agent left a business card for Charles Flint, who told The Associated Press he has known Dan J. Sullivan for years as a respected teacher and musician. The FBI visits came after federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over the candidate. The U.S. Department of Justice also pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion . Flint contributed $500 over the summer to what he considered a long-shot campaign, saying he knew Dan J. Sullivan would have expenses and respected him for “throwing his hat in the ring.” Flint said the FBI agent asked his son, who works at the dealership, whether Flint felt he had been “misled” about which candidate he was supporting. “I don’t feel like I’ve been misled at all,” Flint, who has been out of town, told the AP in a telephone interview, adding he had no intention of calling the agent but would “let him waste his time trying to track me down.” “I don’t think there’s any confusion,” he said, adding he intends to rank Democrat Mary Peltola first on his ballot, followed by Dan J. Sullivan. “Everybody knows who the incumbent is.” Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage the federal investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” Two different FBI agents were dispatched to Sitka to conduct a brief interview at the doorstep of another donor. That donor, who asked that their name not be published given the ongoing investigation, said the agents asked whether the contribution had been made to the Sullivan the donor intended. The conversation lasted about five minutes, the donor told the AP. The donor said the agents were “scrupulously polite” and emphasized that the conversation was entirely voluntary. Yet another donor, Pat Campbell, of Groton, Massachusetts, said a couple of FBI agents came to her door Friday and spoke with her husband. “They said they were from the FBI and investigating fraud in election contributions,” Campbell wrote in a text message to AP. “No, we had not been defrauded. We knew to whom we had contributed.” The developments come just days before Tuesday’s ranked choice general election in a potentially pivotal race in which Peltola, a former congresswoman, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. At a campaign rally in Anchorage on Friday, Peltola again denied involvement in any plan to place candidates on the ballot to detract from the incumbent senator. She said she was “deeply offended” by the allegations, which she called “garbage” and part of a “smear campaign” to suppress turnout on the eve of the election. “I know I can beat Dan Sullivan. I do not need any help winning this race,” she told a small group of campaign volunteers at an Anchorage aviation museum. ___ Mustian reported from New York. Associated Press writer Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/fbi-visits-dan-j-sullivan-041854344.html

item.title: Kamala Harris urges a 'too big to rig' turnout for the midterms and tees off on Trump
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ATLANTA (AP) — Two years after Kamala Harris lost the presidential election to Donald Trump , she still delights Democratic donors and activists with jabs against him, saying the Republican is “callous, corrupt and incompetent” and calling him the “decorator in chief” for his White House renovations and gold adornments. But the former vice president also has plenty to say about what her party, the electorate and the country should do next as she also considers whether to run again. “This is the moment where we turn that anger into action,” Harris said more than once during a busy schedule in the final stretch of the midterm campaign. Harris campaigned for candidates across seven states, ending with a recent two-day visit to Georgia. It was, in parts, the kind of nostalgic tour seen from Barack Obama and Bill Clinton — two-term presidents whose last campaigns are behind them — and the barnstorming from potential future contenders such as Govs. Gavin Newsom of California and Andy Beshear of Kentucky or U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. As the first Black woman elected to nationwide office, Harris urged fellow Black Americans to “honor the ancestors” with their votes but she also has become unapologetically “transactional” by demanding more from politicians. Harris, a California senator before joining Joe Biden on the 2020 ticket, also pushed fellow Democrats to govern aggressively and she called for “structural work” that she said was necessary to reinvigorate American democracy: U.S. Supreme Court expansion, statehood for the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, and reconsideration of the Electoral College. “I think she’s hitting all the right notes,” said Melinda Johnson, a retired nurse who attended a Fulton County Democratic Party fundraising gala that Harris headlined in Atlanta. Harris made it to early presidential primary states , including Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan. She also went to Mississippi, not exactly a hotbed of presidential politics, on behalf of U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom. “The South is in play,” she said. “When Democrats invest in the South, we can win in the South.” In Georgia, Harris delved into civil rights history as she accused the U.S. Supreme Court of “backdoor racism” with its decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and allow Republicans to redraw boundaries for congressional districts that now elect nonwhite lawmakers. “Ruthlessness” is key, she said at the Democratic dinner in Atlanta. “Not ruthlessness in the sense of cruelty … but in our willingness to use our power to deliver on our commitments.” Democrats, she said, “can no longer let process stand in the way of progress.” Throughout her stops, Harris nodded implicitly at her loss to Trump. “You know we’ve been spending the last year and a half, so many of us, going through a range of emotions,” she told students. “Anger, depression, sadness, frustration, a sense of helplessness and powerlessness.” Warning that Trump could try to meddle in Tuesday's election, she echoed one of the president's own mantras to encourage people to vote. “In this case,” she said at Atlanta’s Elizabeth Baptist Church, “we just need to turn out in really large numbers that would be too big to rig.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/kamala-harris-urges-too-big-151418023.html

item.title: El-Sayed campaign wants Stevens to stay away after day of back-and-forth barbs
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
TRAVERSE CITY, MICHIGAN — Michigan's Democratic coalition is fragmenting in real time days before a critical Senate election. After it seemed like former primary rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens might finally appear together, they’re back to sniping at each other. And it could hardly come at a worse moment as Democrats look to unite behind El-Sayed and hold on to a pivotal Senate seat. El-Sayed’s campaign is asking Stevens to stay away from all future campaign events in the closing days of the race, two people familiar with the decision, who were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive campaign dynamics, told POLITICO. She should stay away “as not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” one of the people said. The brushoff capped a day of the two lobbing increasingly pointed statements back and forth at each other, frustrating Democrats who say the infighting risks imperiling a state the party can hardly afford to lose as they try to flip control of the Senate. “I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing. This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes,” Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who was squeezed out of the Democratic primary by the two other candidates, told CNN earlier on Friday, before El-Sayed issued his response. “People are not talking about ads. They are not talking about Haley Stevens. They are talking about the price of gas and groceries.” Stevens did not immediately respond to a question on if she will now stay off the trail, and did not respond to an earlier question about whether her appearance was contingent on him apologizing. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to comment. El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens in a bitter and hard-fought primary in August that exposed division over support for Israel. The seat now held by the retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is crucial to Democratic hopes to take control of the Senate. Stevens and El Sayed have not campaigned together since a post-primary unity breakfast, but appeared on the verge of doing so earlier on Friday. Stevens initially said she would appear alongside El-Sayed and South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn at a church in Detroit on Sunday. But she said she expected the Democratic nominee to apologize for some of his past comments and condemn an ad run by an outside group supporting him that she described as antisemitic. The ad featured a conversation in a grocery store where a woman told a man they couldn't buy eggs because they had to set aside money for “killing Palestinians.” El-Sayed’s campaign had previously noted he was not affiliated with the ad. In response, El-Sayed did not touch on the ad or his past comments on Israel, instead saying that his campaign “has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing” and that that focus “is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70 [million] in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens.” “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said. Privately, Democrats are frustrated — some with Stevens. “Every Democrat was singing the same tune but now, because one person is tone deaf, the whole choir is thrown off,” said a Michigan Democratic operative who is not directly working for El-Sayed’s campaign. Some Democrats tried to downplay the fight heading into the final days of the race. “There’s been a lot of efforts to coalesce Democrats, both from Abdul and from the congresswoman. I think everybody's on the same page of Democrats just beating Mike Rogers," said Joe Tate, a state representative from Detroit who supported Stevens in the primary and is now backing El-Sayed. But he acknowledged that "when you have people that have competed through a primary, I know it can always have those lingering effects." Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg urged Democrats to come together to support El-Sayed. “I've never met somebody who I agree with on 100 percent of everything,” Buttigieg told reporters while campaigning in the state for House candidate Callie Barr on Friday. “But when our health care is at stake, when a chance to have a more affordable everyday life is at stake, the choice is clear: Mike Rogers has disqualified himself.” Republicans have sought to play up the Democratic divisions. Rogers, in a Friday evening post on X , called Stevens a “courageous leader” and said she was “absolutely right” to call on El-Sayed to apologize. “I agree with her and my campaign is about being there, showing up and defending these communities and all Michiganders,” Rogers said. President Donald Trump, at a Friday night rally in Daytona, Florida, had a characteristically blunt message: "If you're Black, or if you're Jewish, and you vote for Abdul, you're not smart,” he said. Stevens’ comments so close to the pivotal election left some Democrats wondering what her goal was. “If you are someone with a large platform — whether you are, say, an outgoing member of Congress or an out-of-state streamer — who genuinely wants Abdul El-Sayed to become the next U.S. Senator from the state of Michigan and for Democrats to take back the Senate and put a meaningful check on Donald Trump, before you speak publicly I would implore you to ask yourself ‘is what I’m doing actually helping, or am I just seeking attention?’,” Democratic operative Adam Carlson, who has polled for a pro El-Sayed super PAC, wrote on X . Sophia Cai contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/30/el-sayed-stevens-senate-race-fight-01144423

item.title: The AI sell-off is exposing the risks of betting on Wall Street’s favorite stocks
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Wall Street analysts spent 2026 piling Buy ratings onto the AI build-out. The stocks they ignored have done better. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) stocks with the biggest share of analyst Buy ratings have trailed those with the smallest share for most of the year, according to Piper Sandler chief investment strategist Michael Kantrowitz. Measured year over year, it's the third-worst stretch in Piper's data going back to 1995. "The Sell Side's MOST favored stocks have underperformed their LEAST favored stocks for the majority of 2026," Kantrowitz wrote in a note to clients Wednesday. This week showed what that looks like. Alphabet had its worst month in history , Intel had its worst day since 1974 , and the Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) suffered its biggest daily drop since June as Big Tech's results revived worries about AI spending. Add it up, and the AI trade has lost about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations, including about $1.6 trillion on Friday alone. Nvidia and Alphabet, two of Piper's favorites, shed about $835 billion each, roughly a third of the total. Yahoo Finance The rest of the market has held up. The other 625 large US stocks in Yahoo Finance's count gained about $1.3 trillion over the same stretch, led by Eli Lilly ( LLY ), Walmart ( WMT ) and Exxon Mobil ( XOM ). It's the slump in Wall Street's favorites, playing out in a single month. Piper picks both groups from the top and bottom of each of the index's 11 sectors, so this isn't tech against everything else. Only two slumps ran deeper, in 2001-02 and 2010. Both came near big turning points in the market, the first as the tech bubble deflated and the second as stocks recovered from the financial crisis. Piper Sandler, Yahoo Finance Why this hits more portfolios than you'd think Most investors own Wall Street's favorites whether they picked them or not. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) are among the biggest weights in the S&P 500, so any index fund or 401(k) that tracks it leans on their fortunes. The slump also shows how a crowded idea can work against investors. When nearly every analyst already loves a stock, much of the good news is in the price, and there are few new buyers left to win over. A disappointment then stings. That's what the favorites are running into. Six of the nine names on Piper's list are down this year, from Alphabet and power producer Vistra ( VST ) to Wynn Resorts ( WYNN ) and Take-Two Interactive ( TTWO ). The exceptions are three AI build-out names: Nvidia, Arista Networks ( ANET ), and Comfort Systems ( FIX ). Meanwhile, nearly all of the least-loved stocks are up, led by steady names like Kenvue ( KVUE ) and Illinois Tool Works ( ITW ). As a group, though, they've only roughly kept pace with the S&P 500. This is less about the laggards running than about the favorites falling. Six of the nine stocks with the most analyst Buy ratings are down this year. Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace A rough week for the AI trade It looked very different in the spring, when Piper's favorites were up nearly 18% on average, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Then the AI trade began to unwind. It crushed the companies leading the data center build-out first, and this week it reached the megacaps. That included the biggest one-day drop in market value in Alphabet's history on Thursday, after its third quarter results. Amazon ( AMZN ) and Intel ( INTC ) led tech lower Friday after their own reports, as Amazon's AI build-out pushed its cash burn to a record . "The AI beta-bubble appears to have already burst!" Kantrowitz wrote. He means the most volatile AI stocks, those with a high beta , which swing more than the market. That doesn't mean the AI trade is over. Kantrowitz expects investors to move toward beaten-down AI companies with stronger businesses as earnings growth slows. In other words, they're getting pickier about which part of AI they pay for. "We do not expect a return to an AI-driven market led by the most speculative (i.e., lower quality) stocks," Kantrowitz wrote.
